claims.text: Increasing compositional complexity increases atomic-size mismatch and lattice distortion in single-phase high-entropy alloys.
Lattice distortion is the dominant factor governing hardness and strength in single-phase high-entropy alloys.
Chemical heterogeneity produces a spatially varying, rugged energy landscape in concentrated multicomponent alloys.
A rugged energy landscape impedes dislocation motion and contributes to alloy strength.
A homogenized, annealed FCC CoCrFeNi alloy can provide a uniform, single-phase starting microstructure with minimized extrinsic defects.
Incrementally adding or varying elements can increase atomic-size mismatch while preserving an otherwise constant single-phase microstructure.
The proposed mechanism applies below the onset of phase separation or significant chemical ordering.
Lattice distortion itself generates the rugged energy landscape affecting dislocation mobility.
Enhanced lattice distortion creates local stress fields that act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Concentrated multicomponent compositions can elevate lattice resistance to dislocation motion relative to conventional metals and dilute solutions.
The strengthening effect is an amplified form of solid-solution strengthening caused by high compositional complexity.
Increasing measured lattice distortion will produce a monotonic increase in hardness and tensile yield strength relative to a lower-distortion baseline.
Strengthening will scale with atomic-size mismatch up to the limit of single-phase stability.
A binary or ternary solid solution has less lattice distortion and a more uniform dislocation-energy landscape than the proposed HEA.
At elevated temperatures, thermal activation reduces the strengthening contribution from lattice distortion.
Phase transformations or significant short-range ordering introduce strengthening mechanisms in addition to lattice distortion.
Local chemical ordering and dislocation-core effects may also influence hardness and strength.

Failure to observe a statistically significant, monotonic strength increase with increasing measured distortion under single-phase conditions would falsify the proposed dominance of lattice distortion.
